title: Anytime-CBU: Adaptive Rollout Allocation for Consequence-Based Utility Scoring

contributions.purpose: Reduces the computational cost of Consequence-Based Utility (CBU) scoring, whose uniform rollout allocation wastes compute on candidates whose quality is clear after few rollouts.
contributions.mechanism: Anytime-CBU reformulates CBU scoring as a best-arm identification (BAI) problem and applies LUCB-style adaptive allocation with Beta-posterior confidence bounds, arm elimination, and early stopping.
contributions.evaluation: Evaluated on RealMath with two solver models (Qwen2.5-Math-7B and DeepSeek-R1-7B) against Uniform-CBU.
contributions.domain: LLM evaluation / test-time compute for mathematical reasoning
contributions.source_quote: We reformulate CBU scoring as a best-arm identification problem and propose Anytime-CBU with LUCB-style adaptive allocation.

contributions.purpose: Establishes empirically whether adaptive allocation actually delivers the intended cost reduction for CBU scoring.
contributions.mechanism: Comprehensive experiments on RealMath comparing Anytime-CBU with Uniform-CBU on selection quality and rollout budget across two solver models.
contributions.evaluation: Anytime-CBU preserves selection quality (overlapping 95% confidence intervals with Uniform-CBU) but achieves only 0-2% rollout reduction, far below the target of at least 50%.
contributions.domain: LLM evaluation / test-time compute for mathematical reasoning
contributions.source_quote: We conduct comprehensive experiments on RealMath with two solver models, demonstrating that Anytime-CBU preserves selection quality but fails to achieve meaningful cost reduction.

contributions.purpose: Explains why the adaptive approach fails, exposing a structural mismatch between BAI assumptions and CBU problem characteristics.
contributions.mechanism: Root-cause analysis of RealMath candidate utility distributions showing flat utility landscapes that make the LUCB stopping condition unsatisfiable within practical budgets.
contributions.evaluation: Identifies flat utility landscapes as the structural root cause of the unsatisfiable LUCB stopping condition, explaining the 0-2% rollout reduction.
contributions.domain: LLM evaluation / test-time compute for mathematical reasoning
contributions.source_quote: We identify the root cause: flat utility landscapes make the LUCB stopping condition unsatisfiable, revealing a structural mismatch between BAI assumptions and CBU problem characteristics.

contributions.purpose: Shows adaptive allocation still has value for ranking even when early stopping fails.
contributions.mechanism: Comparison of adaptive allocation against random allocation at matched rollout cost.
contributions.evaluation: Adaptive allocation outperforms random allocation at matched cost, suggesting intelligent resource allocation matters even without early stopping gains.
contributions.domain: LLM evaluation / test-time compute for mathematical reasoning
contributions.source_quote: We show that adaptive allocation provides ranking benefits even without early stopping, outperforming random allocation at matched cost.

self_declared_provenance.quote: We hypothesize that CBU scoring can be reformulated as a best-arm identification (BAI) problem, where each candidate solution is an arm and each rollout provides a Bernoulli reward (success or failure on a neighbor problem).
Unlike these methods that target answer agreement in self-consistency, our work addresses utility-based scoring where rewards are Bernoulli outcomes from neighbor problem solving.

We adapt this framework to CBU scoring, treating each candidate solution as an arm and each rollout as a pull with Bernoulli reward. However, as our experiments reveal, the effectiveness of BAI approaches depends critically on the utility landscape characteristics.
